title: Electric and Magnetic Forces
seo_title: Grade 8 Electric and Magnetic Forces Worksheets: Charges, Magnets, Fields and Electromagnets
standard_text: Ask questions about data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electric and magnetic forces.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on electric and magnetic forces (NGSS MS-PS2-3, MS-PS2-5): charges and poles, fields acting at a distance, and factors that make electromagnets stronger. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Like charges and like poles repel.
key_sub: Electric and magnetic forces act through fields. They are stronger when objects are closer, with more charge or more current.
body_html:
How to think about it

Electric forces act between charged objects: like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Magnetic forces act between magnets and on iron, nickel, cobalt and steel: like poles repel, opposite poles attract.

These forces act at a distance through fields. Iron filings and compasses show a magnetic field.

Strength depends on: distance (closer → stronger), amount of charge or magnet strength, and for an electromagnet the current, number of coils and an iron core.

Example

Two balloons both have a negative charge. What happens?

Like charges.

Answer: They repel.

Example

An electromagnet with 20 coils lifts 8 clips. What will 40 coils likely do?

More coils → stronger.

Answer: lift more clips

Common mistakes

  • Thinking like charges or like poles attract.
  • Thinking magnets attract every metal.
  • Thinking forces need contact. Fields act at a distance.

faq.q: What affects the strength of an electromagnet?
faq.a: The amount of current, the number of coils of wire and whether there is an iron core.

faq.q: Can electric and magnetic forces act without touching?
faq.a: Yes. Charged objects and magnets have fields that push or pull on other objects at a distance.

faq.q: Why don't magnets attract aluminum cans?
faq.a: Magnets only attract a few metals such as iron, nickel, cobalt and steel. Aluminum is not one of them.

c: a magnetic field around the wire
items.e: This is how electromagnets work.
